summary: Describes APEX, an extensible, asynchronous message relaying service for application layer programs. It provides a best-effort application-level delivery mesh that other services build on. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: APEX was meant to be a postal service for programs, passing notes along from one to another. It never caught on and is historic.

questions: what is the application exchange core
subtitle: An extensible messaging service for applications to exchange data through a relaying mesh.

tldr.problem: Applications need a way to send messages asynchronously to other applications with flexible delivery guarantees and options, without building a full reliable transport layer.
tldr.mechanism: APEX provides a best-effort datagram service where applications attach to a relaying mesh, send data messages to named endpoints, and can request processing options to alter delivery behavior.
tldr.outcome: APEX was proposed as an extensible messaging backbone but never achieved widespread adoption and is now historic.

today: RFC 3340 is now Historic. APEX was designed as a flexible messaging service but never achieved significant adoption in the Internet. The protocol is not actively used or developed.

sections.title: What APEX Does
sections.content:
APEX (Application Exchange) is a messaging service that lets application programs send messages to each other asynchronously over a network. Unlike email or file transfer, APEX focuses on application-to-application messaging with a set of principles that applications can customize.

At its core, APEX offers a best-effort datagram service, similar to how postcards work: the message gets sent, but there is no guarantee it arrives, no guarantee it arrives in order, and no guarantee it does not arrive multiple times. Applications that need certainty should use a different protocol. But for many applications, including instant messaging and event notification systems, best-effort is enough.
sections.plainLanguage: APEX lets programs post letters to each other. It does not promise the letter arrives, which is fine for many things like news updates.

sections.title: How It Works: Endpoints and Relays
sections.content:
APEX has two kinds of participants. Endpoints are the programs sending and receiving messages. Relays are servers in administrative domains that forward messages between endpoints.

When an application wants to send a message, it attaches to the relaying mesh using a BEEP profile (an underlying protocol for structured conversations over TCP). The application identifies itself as an endpoint (for example, fred@example.com), then sends data messages specifying an originator, one or more recipients, optional content, and optional processing options.

Messages travel from endpoint to relay to relay to endpoint. Relays check access policies, forward messages to other relays or endpoints, and may apply options like queuing or timing constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Your program talks to a relay server, tells it a name (like fred@example.com), and then says 'send this message to barney@example.com'. The relay finds Barney and delivers it.

sections.title: The Four Message Operations
sections.content:
APEX defines four kinds of messages an application exchanges with a relay: attach, bind, terminate, and data.

Attach registers an application as an endpoint on the relaying mesh. In the endpoint-relay mode, the application initiates, and the relay responds with success or an error code. Bind is similar but used in relay-relay mode, where relays identify themselves to each other by administrative domain (for example, example.com).

Terminate releases an attachment or binding. Data is the actual message: it specifies an originator endpoint, one or more recipient endpoints, a content reference (either a URI or inline XML), and optional processing options. Relays return success or an error code.
sections.plainLanguage: Your program says 'I am Fred' (attach). Later it says 'send this message to Barney' (data). Then it says 'goodbye' (terminate). Very straightforward.

sections.title: Options: Changing the Default Behavior
sections.content:
The core service is best-effort, but APEX lets applications request options to change that. An option is specified in an attach or data message with attributes controlling which relay processes it, whether it is mandatory, and its transaction ID.

Options can apply to different scopes: per-data, per-originator, or per-recipient. The statusRequest option is defined in the core RFC and asks relays to send status reports back to the originator. Other options are defined in companion RFCs (3341 for access control, 3342 for advanced options like timing constraints and data queuing).

The option mechanism makes APEX extensible: new options can be registered with IANA without changing the core protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add special requests to your message, like 'tell me when it arrives' or 'wait for the person to be online before delivering'. That is what options do.

sections.title: Security: Authentication, Access, and Confidentiality
sections.content:
APEX delegates authentication to BEEP, the underlying protocol. A relay can require the application to authenticate itself before allowing operations. Authorization is a local matter: the relay provisioning decides which BEEP peer identities are allowed to attach as which APEX endpoints.

The access service (RFC 3341) provides fine-grained control over which endpoints can send data to which endpoints. Confidentiality is the application's responsibility: if data is sensitive, the application should encrypt it before sending, because APEX relays do not encrypt hop-by-hop (they forward the opaque content unchanged). MIME-based security like OpenPGP or S/MIME can be used for end-to-end protection.

Relays must support TLS for hop-by-hop encryption and SASL/DIGEST-MD5 for authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: APEX does not encrypt messages itself, so if you send something private, encrypt it first. Relays can have rules about who is allowed to send to whom.
